title: Moved River, Leased Hill: Kobe's Settlement and Meriken Park
standfirst: Kobe was a village of sand and fields, picked for the foreign settlement because there was little there to disturb. A British engineer's leased grid rose by the shore in 1868; residents climbed the hillside above it, a flooding river was diverted to make room, and the harbor grew into today's Meriken Park. This dossier reads all three through what still stands.

sections.heading: A fan of gravel between the mountain and the sea

paragraphs.text: The study area is a narrow shelf where the streams running off Mount Rokko spread into a fan of gravel and sand, flatten into a river floodplain, and then meet a shoreline that has been almost entirely built out into the bay. Two rivers bounded the village the foreigners would inherit: the Koi-gawa (鯉川) to the west and the Ikuta-gawa (生田川) to the east, both fed by short, steep catchments that ran dry in summer and flooded without warning after rain. Kobe City's own 1925 history describes the ground between them as mostly dry field and paddy, with beach sand along the shore, a scatter of burial mounds, and the boat landing of Kobe village inside what would become the settlement.

The Ikuta River had a long literary life before it had a commercial one. An 1897 Kobe guidebook strings together a chain of classical poems on the river and on 生田磯, the strand in front of Ikuta Shrine, which it says older books place on the very coast later built up as the settlement. It also recalls the medieval tale, taken from the Yamato Monogatari, of the maiden of Unai and the two suitors who fought for her over this river until she drowned herself between them: a story much older than any consulate. To the west lay Hyogo, already a working port under the Taira and the Edo-period kitamae-bune trade; Kobe was chosen for the new foreign settlement precisely because it was the emptier, less-developed ground of the two, a point the settlement's own historical association still makes today.

sections.heading: A settlement built in less than a year

paragraphs.text: Kobe's port opened to foreign trade on 1 January 1868 (Keio 3, 12th month, 7th day), but the settlement that gave the port its foreign quarter was still a building site. The shogunate had only finished buying the land in the seventh month of 1867 by the old calendar, about four months before the port opened, and Kobe City's history, quoting a letter from the Hyogo magistrate Shibata Hyuga-no-kami, records that construction was about seventy percent complete by 16 December 1867; the Japan Chronicle's jubilee history, quoted in the same volume, says the settlement had still not reached the house-building stage by the end of May 1868. The shogunate's own accounts, reproduced in the same city history, put its total outlay above 220,000 ryo: land compensation, grading at one ryo a tsubo, a stone seawall costing 37,500 ryo, drains, and landfill costing more again.

The man who gave the settlement its famous grid was a British civil engineer, J. W. Hart, working to European planning practice: one hundred and twenty-six lots, straight streets, drains and street trees, sold to foreign leaseholders (never owners — Japan kept the freehold) in four auctions between September 1868 and February 1873. A contemporary English-language newspaper is said to have called it the best-planned foreign settlement in the East, and the grid it drew is still the street plan of the Kyu-Kyoryuchi business district today. The settlement stayed under foreign municipal self-government, paid for by its own residents' land tax, until Japan's revised treaties took effect and Japan resumed full administration of the area on 17 July 1899.

Five weeks after the port opened, the unfinished settlement produced Japan's first serious diplomatic crisis with the Western powers. On the eleventh day of the first month by the old calendar (4 February 1868), a column of troops from the Bizen (Okayama) domain, under the retainers Ikeda Ise and Heki Tatewaki, was marching through the Kobe road when foreign nationals crossed or interrupted its line of march; shots were fired. Kobe City's own documentary volume reproduces the exchange of notes that followed within a day: the resident foreign ministers warned Japan's new government on 5 February that unless the affair were settled to every power's satisfaction it could bring war on the whole country, not just Bizen, and foreign warships seized a Japanese steamer lying in Hyogo harbor as a guarantee. Bizen's own report of 7 February, also preserved in this volume, gives a different emphasis, blaming "unreasonable conduct by the foreigners" for the exchange of fire — a reminder that the Japanese and Western accounts of the Kobe Incident were not the same story even at the time.

The imperial court's representative, Higashikuze Michitomi, met the envoys of the six treaty powers in Hyogo on 8 February to settle how the settlement would be policed from then on. The affair itself was closed a few weeks later at the cost of one life: a library reference file assembled from more than a dozen histories and biographical dictionaries records that Taki Zenzaburo, the Bizen officer held responsible, committed seppuku at Eifuku-ji temple in Hyogo on 2 March 1868, watched by representatives of the foreign powers and by Japanese officials that included the young Ito Hirobumi. It did what the diplomats needed: no warship fired on Kobe.

sections.heading: Moving a river, naming a street

paragraphs.text: The Ikuta River was the settlement's other problem. Kobe City recalls that the old river normally carried no more than a trickle but turned into a torrent after any prolonged rain, repeatedly damaging the low ground on its western bank where the foreign lots lay; the foreign residents pressed hard enough that the new Meiji government agreed to move it. A 1942 city guidebook, drawing on the engineering record, dates the decision to the second month of 1871 by the old calendar, construction from the third month, and completion in the sixth — a new channel about 1.8 km long and some 18 m wide dug well to the east of the old one. The old riverbed and its banks, more than 41,700 tsubo of land, were then auctioned in 1873; the city guide names the winning bidders as Arimoto Akira of Wakayama and Kano Soshichi of Kobe, though it is Kano's name the neighborhood still carries.

Kano laid an eighteen-meter road down the middle of the old riverbed at a time when an ordinary Kobe street was 3.6 m wide, and built house lots on either side; the district took his name, Kano-cho, and his road is Kobe's Flower Road today. A 1922 planning survey lists the river-moving as one of a run of large works — the settlement's own land readjustment in 1873, new roads the same year, the Osaka-Kobe railway in 1874, and the Hyogo Shinkawa canal, dug through the old port at Hyogo, in 1875 — and opens its own chapter by noting that Kobe had grown in fifty-odd years into Japan's third-largest city. The rebuilt Ikuta channel was itself culverted in 1931 for road space, then reopened as open water after the 1938 flood proved the culvert a liability.

sections.heading: Up the hill, along the water

paragraphs.text: By the 1880s the settlement's original lots were full of offices and warehouses, and foreign residents who worked there began building houses on the gentler, better-aired slope above it, in what is now Kitano-cho and Yamamoto-dori. Kobe City dates the move to around 1887 and says more than two hundred Western- and Japanese-style houses eventually stood on the hillside; war and later redevelopment cut that to about eighty Western-style buildings by the time of the 1995 earthquake. The Agency for Cultural Affairs designated 9.3 hectares of the hillside an Important Preservation District for Groups of Traditional Buildings on 10 April 1980, recognizing, among others, the houses today shown to the public as the Weathercock House and the former Hassam and Hunter residences.

Down on the water, the harbor grew wharf by wharf out from the settlement's shore. The pier that gave today's park its name was built in 1868 as a landing wharf for foreign cargo, near where the American consulate stood; Japanese ears heard "America" as "meriken," and Meriken Hatoba — the American Wharf — stuck as its name. The Naka pier immediately to its east, built out further into the bay, was completed in 1938. Trade statistics that Kobe City itself published year after year through the Meiji and Taisho eras — foreign and coastal cargo tonnage, ship arrivals, bonded-warehouse space — chart a port that grew, within the same fifty years as Kano's road and the settlement's own land sales, into one of the busiest in Asia.

sections.heading: Flood, fire and a broken quay

paragraphs.text: On 5 July 1938 the Ikuta and the other short rivers off Rokko produced the worst disaster in Kobe's modern history. Kobe City's own 1939 flood record describes rain building from the evening of 3 July — 165 mm fell in the twenty hours to 4 pm the next day — with landslides already breaking out across the hillside wards; a second, far heavier burst began before dawn on the 5th and peaked between 10 and 11 a.m., when 47.6 mm fell in a single hour and 134.4 mm in three. The Toga River's embankment in Nada had already given way the previous afternoon. Debris flows the city called "mountain tsunami" swept down every steep valley behind the built-up area at once, and the first report of catastrophic damage reached city hall at about 10 a.m. on the 5th from Minato ward, where two rivers had burst their banks together.

The same 1939 volume counts Kobe's losses at 378 dead and 134 missing, 5,961 houses swept away or destroyed and a further 26,921 half-destroyed, and sets them beside the damage Osaka and Kyoto had suffered in the Muroto typhoon less than four years earlier. The city itself estimated that around half a million cubic meters of mud and boulders had come down off the mountain. Seven years later the war reached the same streets: Kobe City's official count lists five major American air raids in 1945 — 4 February, 17 March, 11 May, 5 June and 6 August — that between them killed 7,524 people by the city's current figure, injured almost 17,000, and destroyed more than 142,000 houses, forcing over half a million residents from their homes.

The waterfront itself was made twice more after the war. In 1987, marking the anniversary of the port's opening, the city filled the sixteen hectares of water between the old Meriken wharf and the 1938 Naka pier to create Meriken Park, setting the Kobe Maritime Museum and, later, the Kobe Port Tower on ground that had been open harbor within living memory. Then, at 5:46 a.m. on 17 January 1995, the Great Hanshin-Awaji earthquake tore through the reclaimed waterfront along with the rest of the city; this dossier's companion Basic brief gives the district's memorials and the city's official casualty figures. The port authority left about sixty meters of the shattered Meriken wharf exactly as the earthquake had cracked and tilted it, opening the site as the Port of Kobe Earthquake Memorial Park in July 1997 and renewing its displays in January 2025 for the disaster's thirtieth anniversary.

Three layers are still there to be read on the ground. The old settlement's grid of streets and its scale of blocks, laid out by Hart in 1868, survive under the banks and offices of the Kyu-Kyoryuchi district even though almost every individual building has been rebuilt. Flower Road, running north from Sannomiya, follows the riverbed Kano Soshichi bought in 1873, and Kano-cho still carries his name. And up on the hill, the houses of Kitano-cho and Yamamoto-dori mark the line foreign residents drew in the 1880s between the settlement where they worked and the slope where they preferred to live — a division the whole city has since grown around.

timeline.what: Kobe/Hyogo opens to foreign trade; the settlement itself is still unfinished.
Bizen domain troops and foreign nationals exchange fire on the Kobe road (the Kobe Incident).
Taki Zenzaburo commits seppuku at Eifuku-ji, Hyogo, before foreign witnesses, closing the incident.
J. W. Hart's settlement grid of 126 lots is sold to foreign leaseholders in four auctions.
The Ikuta River is diverted east over a few months; the old bed is auctioned in 1873 and becomes Kano-cho.
The Hyogo Shinkawa canal is completed through the old port at Hyogo.
Foreign residents begin building houses on the Kitano hillside above the settlement.
The foreign settlement's special administration ends; Japan resumes full control of the district.
The Great Hanshin flood kills 378 and leaves 134 missing in Kobe by the city's own count.
The Naka pier, east of Meriken wharf, is completed.
Five major US air raids (Feb, Mar, May, Jun, Aug) kill 7,524 by Kobe City's current figure.
Kitano-cho and Yamamoto-dori are designated a national preservation district for traditional buildings.
Meriken Park opens on 16 ha reclaimed between the old Meriken wharf and Naka pier.
The Great Hanshin-Awaji earthquake (17 Jan 1995) damages the wharf; the Port of Kobe Earthquake Memorial Park preserving it opens in July 1997.

walk.name: Kyu-Kyoryuchi (Old Settlement) streets
walk.what: Walk the grid of banks and trading-company buildings between Kaigan-dori and the Daimaru department store; the street widths and block sizes are still J. W. Hart's of 1868, even though almost every building standing today was rebuilt after 1945 or 1995.

walk.name: Ikuta Shrine and Flower Road
walk.ja: 生田神社・フラワーロード
walk.what: Ikuta Shrine stands near the old river celebrated in classical verse long before 1868; Flower Road, a few minutes' walk to the east, follows the riverbed the city abandoned in 1871 and Kano Soshichi built over in 1873.

walk.name: Kano-cho street grid
walk.what: The blocks either side of Flower Road, laid out on the dry riverbed at an unusually generous 18 m road width for 1873, still bear Kano's name.

walk.name: Meriken Park and the Port of Kobe Earthquake Memorial Park
walk.ja: メリケンパーク・神戸港震災メモリアルパーク
walk.what: The park fills the water once open between the 1868 Meriken wharf and the 1938 Naka pier; at its edge, roughly sixty meters of quay wall are left exactly as the 1995 earthquake cracked and tilted them.

walk.name: Kobe Maritime Museum and Kobe Port Tower
walk.ja: 神戸海洋博物館・神戸ポートタワー
walk.what: Standing on filled ground that was harbor water within living memory, the museum sets Kobe's port history — sail, steam, container — beside the wharves it describes.

walk.name: Kitano-cho and Yamamoto-dori (Kitano ijinkan-gai)
walk.ja: 北野町・山本通（北野異人館街）
walk.what: Climb from the settlement to the houses foreign residents built on this slope from about 1887, among them the Weathercock House and the former Hassam and Hunter residences, within the 9.3 ha preservation district designated in 1980.

deepResearchLeads.what: Minute books and land records of the settlement's own foreign municipal council (1868–1899), and the original J. W. Hart plan and land-auction records
deepResearchLeads.where: Kobe City Archives (神戸市文書館) and Kobe City Museum (神戸市立博物館), which holds the settlement plan reproduced online
deepResearchLeads.how: Search the museum's online collection first (heritage id 365270 for the settlement plan), then contact the City Archives' reading room for the council's own minute books and leasehold registers by lot number.

deepResearchLeads.what: Full consular correspondence on the Kobe Incident from the British, French, American, Dutch, Prussian and Italian legations
deepResearchLeads.where: Japan's Diplomatic Archives (外交史料館) for the Japanese side; the UK National Archives (FO 262 Japan correspondence) and equivalent French, American and Dutch foreign-ministry archives for the foreign side
deepResearchLeads.how: Diplomatic Archives records can be requested by date and file number through its reading room in Tokyo; foreign archives generally take written requests citing the January–February 1868 date range.

deepResearchLeads.what: Mission reports and target photographs for the five 1945 air raids on Kobe
deepResearchLeads.where: US National Archives (NARA): XXI Bomber Command mission folders (RG 18) and US Strategic Bombing Survey files (RG 243)
deepResearchLeads.how: Search the NARA online catalog by date and target city; records are open and reproductions can be ordered remotely.

deepResearchLeads.what: Administrative and engineering records of the 1938 flood relief and the 1936–1947-era river works on the Ikuta and neighboring rivers
deepResearchLeads.where: Hyogo Prefectural Archives and the Kobe City Public Works (土木) records held by the City Archives
deepResearchLeads.how: Search prefectural and city archive catalogues for 水害 and 河川改修 administrative files from 1938–1947; request in advance for reading-room viewing.

deepResearchLeads.what: House-by-house leasehold and rebuilding history of an individual Kitano ijinkan or Kyu-Kyoryuchi lot
deepResearchLeads.where: Kobe District Legal Affairs Bureau (closed land registers, 旧土地台帳) and the City's cultural-heritage section, which holds preservation-district survey reports
deepResearchLeads.how: Request old land registers by lot number at the Legal Affairs Bureau; ask the cultural-heritage section (文化財課) for the building-by-building survey behind the 1980 designation.

caveats: Secondary accounts of the Kobe Incident differ on the nationality of the foreign sailors involved (English or French in different popular retellings); the primary correspondence read for this dossier (S3) says only "foreigners" and does not resolve this.

The 1942 city guidebook (S6) names two successful bidders for the old Ikuta riverbed in 1873, Arimoto Akira and Kano Soshichi, though later tradition and the neighborhood's own name, Kano-cho, remember only Kano.

Casualty figures for the 1938 flood vary between sources depending on whether the count covers Kobe City alone or the wider Hanshin region, and by date of tally; this dossier uses Kobe City's own contemporary count from its 1939 flood record (S4).

The Kitano-cho/Yamamoto-dori preservation district's center lies a short distance north of this dossier's formal study-area box; it is treated here in full because it is inseparable from the settlement's history and named in the district's own title.
